CausalChain: HCC with compromised liver function -> ALBI grade reflects liver reserve (albumin & bilirubin levels) -> ICI therapy imposes additional risk of immune-mediated liver injury -> Continuous digital platforms capture both static and dynamic ALBI variations plus additional biomarkers -> Hybrid machine learning (real-time and retrospective) identifies early subclinical deviations -> Validated threshold changes predict imminent immune-related hepatotoxicity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC patients undergoing ICI therapy, a hybrid monitoring system leveraging continuous digital data—including dynamic ALBI measurements obtained via IoT-connected biosensors, routine static ALBI assessments from EHRs, and additional hepatic (e.g., AST, ALT) and inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, IL-6)—can more accurately predict immune-related hepatotoxicity than conventional static measurements alone. By applying advanced, interpretable machine learning algorithms that integrate both high-frequency temporal data and cross-sectional data, our model aims to establish and validate clinically-relevant threshold shifts in ALBI dynamics that reliably differentiate between baseline hepatic dysfunction and nascent ICI-induced liver injury. This integrated real-time and snapshot data strategy is expected to enable early clinical interventions, optimize dosing strategies, and thereby improve overall patient outcomes.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients often harbor chronic liver dysfunction, making them vulnerable to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy–induced hepatotoxicity. We propose a novel digital monitoring approach that integrates continuously measured ALBI (Albumin-Bilirubin) dynamics with a suite of complementary hepatic and inflammatory biomarkers, enhanced by advanced and explainable machine learning models. Specifically, our methodology combines high-frequency, IoT-enabled biosensor data with static ALBI assessments from electronic health records to robustly differentiate between intrinsic liver function fluctuations and early, subclinical manifestations of ICI-induced liver injury. This hybrid framework (leveraging both real-time and snapshot data) is designed to establish validated threshold shifts that predict impending hepatotoxicity, thereby offering actionable insights for timely dose adjustments and personalized interventions. The approach not only builds upon established ALBI prognostic properties but also exploits contemporary digital health technology to refine early predictive capabilities in a high-risk HCC population.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that continuous, digital tracking of ALBI via machine learning could serve as an early biomarker for ICI-induced liver injury, relying solely on ALBI dynamics to differentiate chronic liver variations from new injury. In the refined hypothesis, we have enhanced the concept by: 1) incorporating additional hepatic and inflammatory biomarkers (e.g., AST, ALT, CRP, IL-6) to supplement ALBI data, thereby addressing the concern that static ALBI assessments already serve as robust prognostic markers; 2) adopting a hybrid approach that combines high-frequency, real-time monitoring with traditional static measures from EHRs, mitigating inherent variability in ALBI readings; and 3) emphasizing the use of advanced, explainable machine learning algorithms to integrate heterogeneous data. Each step of the original causal chain is retained—starting from compromised liver function in HCC, through ALBI’s role in assessing liver reserve, the impact of ICI therapy, to the detection of early subclinical liver injury—but is now reinforced with contemporary data integration methods and additional biomarkers to enhance specificity, validity, and clinical utility.
